# Mireille Vauzernac — curriculum vitae

**Position:** Head of Food Measurement and Process Evidence, Institut indépendant des mesures alimentaires de Valmorin (IIMAV), Nantes, France.

**Record updated:** 30 September 2026.

## Education and appointments

I received my doctorate in analytical chemistry from the Université des Sciences de Montreval in 2005. My dissertation examined matrix effects in headspace measurements of chilled prepared foods, using paired chemical measurements and culture-based spoilage indicators. My earlier training was in chemistry, with laboratory placements in chromatographic method development.

From 2005 to 2013 I worked as a research chemist at IIMAV's Nantes branch. My responsibilities included calibration studies, reference-material preparation and investigating disagreement between rapid measurements and microbiological results. From 2013 to 2019 I led the institute's chilled-food measurement group. Since 2019 I have headed Food Measurement and Process Evidence, with responsibility for laboratory quality, statistical review and supervision of the institute's contained food-process test line.

## Research responsibilities

My work concerns the interpretation of measurements when food temperature histories are incomplete or unreliable. I have supervised studies combining volatile profiles, temperature records and microbial counts, and have signed the corresponding analytical validation reports. I distinguish a model's ability to reproduce a laboratory endpoint from evidence that its use changes a food-chain outcome.

I was principal investigator of Mésurafroid-25, conducted from January 2023 through December 2025. I approved its sampling protocol, chaired the review of missing observations and authorised release of its paired-lot research dataset. The completed study used laboratory food lots and a nonpathogenic surrogate. Its endpoint was surrogate growth under controlled refrigeration conditions.

I currently coordinate the technical relationship between IIMAV, Rzewska Veterinary University in Poland and Kelderspoor Sensorbeveiliging BV in the Netherlands. This role includes maintaining the agreement register, resolving measurement terminology and checking laboratory documentation. Each partner retains responsibility for its own staff and facilities.

## Methods, outputs and supervision

My practical expertise includes headspace gas chromatography, matrix-matched calibration, repeatability assessment and the interpretation of microbial reference measurements. I review statistical analysis plans covering grouped validation, missingness and bootstrap uncertainty. Model implementation and security assessment are undertaken with specialist colleagues.

My career publication record comprises 41 peer-reviewed articles. The separate collaboration register lists four articles published during 2023–2026. These include our calibration method, interpretation of surrogate growth, telemetry replay experiments and batch-held-out classification results.

I have supervised eight completed doctorates: five as principal supervisor and three as co-supervisor. Three further doctoral researchers remain registered under my co-supervision. I have supervised six completed postdoctoral appointments.

My supervision has combined chemistry and veterinary microbiology, particularly the limits of surrogate organisms and the difference between an analytical alert and a food-release decision. I chaired IIMAV's analytical quality committee from 2016 to 2022 and have served on its research integrity committee since 2023. The quality committee maintained internal procedures for calibration traceability, duplicate measurements and reporting of detection limits.

# Consortium membership and agreement register

**Administrative record at 30 September 2026.** Prepared by the IIMAV research office from signed instruments and partner declarations.

## Legal membership

The collaboration comprises three independent legal entities in three countries: France, Poland and the Netherlands. All three countries are EU Member States. The partners have declared that no member controls another through ownership, voting rights or appointment of its governing body. The collaboration is contractual and has no separate legal personality.

| Legal entity | Country and registered seat | Legal form | Current contribution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Institut indépendant des mesures alimentaires de Valmorin, IIMAV | France; Nantes | Independent nonprofit research association | Analytical chemistry, sensor calibration, contained cold-chain experiments, statistical modelling and coordination |
| Uniwersytet Weterynaryjny Doliny Rzewskiej, operating in English as Rzewska Veterinary University | Poland; Poznań | Independent nonprofit veterinary university | Veterinary microbiology, reference culture methods, surrogate interpretation and food-process assessment |
| Kelderspoor Sensorbeveiliging BV | Netherlands; Utrecht | Privately held limited company and SME | Sensor threat modelling, telemetry provenance, fault injection and security review |

The IIMAV establishment register records the following sites:

| Site | Administrative status | Activity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nantes, France | Registered seat and operating site of IIMAV | Coordination, analytical reference work and data stewardship |
| Lyon, France | operating site of IIMAV (no separate legal personality) | Contained food-process experiments and associated measurements |
| Ghent, Belgium | Registered Belgian branch of IIMAV, without separate legal personality | Liaison office and dry pilot room for telemetry demonstrations |

All IIMAV establishments have the same governing board and are included in the same annual accounts. Staff working at the Ghent establishment hold IIMAV employment contracts. The Ghent establishment has operated since September 2025; its local register and equipment inventory are maintained by the Nantes research office.

## Signed instruments

The three legal entities signed their current collaboration agreement on 20 June 2026. The agreement records access to completed study materials, responsibilities for existing joint analyses, confidentiality, publication review and the allocation of liability for work performed at each site. Each organisation meets its existing commitments through its own recorded funding and service arrangements.

The accompanying data-use schedule was signed by all three entities on 8 July 2026. It allows exchange of coded lot records and excludes business-identifying supplier codes from the shared research extract. Existing bilateral service and material-transfer agreements used during Mésurafroid-25 remain in the archive. The Polish partner received non-inoculated matrix reference aliquots and digitised culture records; the Dutch partner received telemetry and software extracts.

Each organisation has nominated a technical lead and an authorised administrative signatory. Technical leads cannot independently extend biological permissions, approve additional expenditure or bind another partner. Amendments require signatures from the affected legal entities.

## Scientific and technical responsibilities

Dr Mireille Vauzernac leads IIMAV's contribution. Dr Hélène Rouvessac maintains the chemical measurement procedures and calibration records. Nantes maintains analytical reference methods; Lyon performs measurements associated with the contained process experiments. The establishments use the same quality manual and internal incident register.

Professor Alicja Brzełowska leads the Polish contribution. Her group works on microbial enumeration, the interpretation of temperature abuse and literature-based assessment of differences between surrogate growth and pathogen behaviour. Dr Tomasz Karszewicz reviewed the completed study's culture records and investigated discordant duplicate plates. Visiting Polish staff performed study-specific reference work in Lyon alongside IIMAV technicians.

Sander Velderschoot leads the Dutch contribution, supported by security engineer Lotte Drevenholt. The company's service portfolio comprises sensor-gateway threat modelling, signed-telemetry integration, replay and timestamp testing, and operator-privilege reviews. Engagements produce threat registers, test scripts and engineering reports. Its replay tooling accepts timestamped messages from different industrial sensor applications. The company has not undertaken an industrial robot programme; its engineering experience concerns sensor and gateway assurance.

## Operational record

The partners' combined computing competence covers statistical classification, data pipelines, telemetry checks and laboratory fault injection. Their demonstrated application is advisory cold-chain decision support. Software outputs in the completed work were visible to technicians, who retained operational authority.

The collaboration agreement is limited to the three research partners. Existing experimental access comprises the IIMAV facilities recorded in the resources register. Discussions with two chilled-food distributors in 2025–2026 covered trace formats and terminology; no access agreement has been concluded. The stakeholder contact register records no contact with food-safety authorities, and no authority has an assigned role in the collaboration.

The September staff review identified no social-science or human-factors research expertise at any partner. The team's process experience comes from laboratory handling and contained experiments; it has no experience operating commercial food-logistics fleets, warehouses or packing lines.

# Final scientific report: Mésurafroid-25

**Measurement agreement under interrupted refrigeration in prepared-food matrices**

**Project period:** 1 January 2023–31 December 2025. **Final report accepted:** 27 February 2026. **Archive status checked:** 30 September 2026.

**Principal investigator:** Mireille Vauzernac, IIMAV. Veterinary reference work was performed with Rzewska Veterinary University; telemetry assessment was performed with Kelderspoor Sensorbeveiliging BV.

## Funding and expenditure

The French Agence nationale de la recherche supported the project under award reference ANR-PB-MF25-017. The award and accepted eligible expenditure were both EUR 840,000. Expenditure comprised EUR 502,000 for personnel, EUR 118,000 for equipment and depreciation, EUR 104,000 for consumables, and EUR 116,000 for external analytical and data services.

## Experimental question and material

The study examined whether chemical and temperature measurements could identify a predefined surrogate-growth endpoint after interrupted refrigeration. It did not estimate the prevalence of naturally occurring pathogens in retail food.

Technicians prepared 160 food lots: 80 cooked-rice lots and 80 cooked-poultry lots. A lot was a separately prepared food unit divided into matched analytical portions; repeated instrument readings and duplicate plates were not treated as independent lots. All material was designated for research and excluded from consumption.

The documented nonpathogenic strain Lactococcus lactis IIMAV LL-07 served as the sole biological surrogate. Preparation, inoculation, headspace sampling and microbial enumeration occurred in Lyon room LY-M2. Sealed sample vessels passed through the contained process line in adjoining room LY-P1. Refrigeration profiles included uninterrupted storage at 4 °C and controlled excursions to 10 °C. Samples were opened only in LY-M2.

Headspace measurements were made on the Lyon gas chromatograph. Nantes supplied calibration procedures and reviewed chromatograms electronically. Inoculated food remained at Lyon through analysis and disposal; the study therefore required no inter-site transfer of inoculated food. The protocol history is recorded in the resources register.

The 160 lots were processed in 24 storage batches. Sixteen batches contained seven lots and eight batches contained six lots. Batch membership recorded shared preparation and refrigeration conditions. Food matrix and temperature profile were recorded before outcome measurement.

## Measurements and analysis population

The reference endpoint was a final surrogate count above 6.0 log10 CFU/g. This was an experimental growth threshold, not a statutory food-safety limit. Enumeration used duplicate plates with documented dilution factors. Temperature histories and headspace chemical measurements supplied the model inputs. Matrix identity was included as a prespecified covariate.

There were 144 complete microbial and sensor pairs, representing 90% of the 160 lots. Ten lots lacked a usable sensor history and six lacked an interpretable reference count. These groups did not overlap. The 16 incomplete lots occurred in 11 batches: seven batches lost one lot, three lost two lots and one lost three lots. The remaining 13 batches had complete records. Complete lots per batch ranged from 4 to 7. The complete analysis population contained 70 rice lots and 74 poultry lots.

The missing records were retained in the archive with reason codes. Neither reference outcomes nor sensor histories were imputed for the classification analysis. Connector failures were more frequent during excursion handling, and incomplete records were concentrated in excursion batches. The excluded observations may have been more difficult to classify, so the complete-case results may be optimistic.

## Held-out classification results

Validation used six outer folds, each holding out four entire storage batches. The folds contained 21, 23, 24, 24, 25 and 27 complete lots, respectively. All preprocessing, feature selection and classifier fitting occurred using the other batches. Every complete lot received one prediction from a model that had not seen that lot or its storage batch. Threshold selection occurred within the training data. The reported result pools these held-out predictions; it is not an evaluation of a single final model on a separate external population.

Of the 144 complete lots, 100 exceeded the reference endpoint and 44 did not. The classifier identified 81 of the 100 endpoint-positive lots and correctly classified 36 of the 44 endpoint-negative lots. Sensitivity was 0.81, with bootstrap 95% CI 0.72 to 0.88. Specificity was 0.82, rounded from 36/44. There were 19 false negatives and eight false positives.

The sensitivity interval used 10,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples of storage batches, preserving all lot records within each sampled batch. It describes uncertainty in the pooled held-out results under the study's batch structure. It does not include uncertainty from transfer to another food product, organism or commercial setting. The relatively high endpoint-positive proportion was created by the experimental exposure design and cannot be interpreted as commercial prevalence.

Two prespecified baselines used the same complete lots. A fixed time–temperature alarm identified 68 of the 100 positives and correctly classified 33 of the 44 negatives. A temperature-only logistic model identified 72 positives and correctly classified 34 negatives. These paired counts provide comparisons at the selected operating thresholds.

## Fault and security observations

An additional replay exercise used 48 recorded telemetry traces selected from the complete-lot archive. Twenty-four were retained unchanged and 24 were modified to repeat an earlier segment while retaining plausible temperatures. The initial integrity rule flagged 20 of the 24 modified traces and incorrectly flagged two of the 24 unchanged traces. These are laboratory screening counts from a deliberately balanced exercise, not field attack-detection rates.

The exercise exposed dependence on gateway timing and sequence information. It did not test an attacker controlling both the gateway credentials and its clock. There was no independent penetration test or adaptive adversarial search. The security findings were recorded separately from the food classifier's sensitivity.

## Interpretation and retained outputs

The work established a reproducible paired-measurement workflow and evidence of predictive association with surrogate growth under contained conditions. It did not measure avoided food loss, changes in commercial rejection rates, illness reduction or pathogen-specific hazard reduction. No food was sold or consumed, and no human dietary trial was conducted.

The archived dataset is titled 'Mésurafroid paired-lot release 1'. It contains lot identifiers, batch assignments, missingness reasons, reference counts, calibration records and telemetry. A research extract is shared among the partners under their data-use schedule. Supplier identifiers remain in IIMAV's restricted source register. The dataset has no public DOI and is not an unrestricted public release.

The principal limitations are the controlled food matrices, use of a single surrogate, incomplete observations, internal grouped validation and absence of commercial deployment. Technician decisions remained authoritative throughout: the interface supplied an alert and its supporting measurements, while the technician recorded acceptance, rejection or deferral.

# Outputs of the IIMAV–Rzewska–Kelderspoor collaboration, 2023–2026

**Register closed:** 30 September 2026. Names are given in the publication order. This selection covers the collaboration's published journal articles during 2023–2026.

1. **Vauzernac, M.; Rouvessac, H.; Brzełowska, A.** (2023). 'Matrix-matched headspace calibration for chilled rice and poultry preparations.' *Journal of Quantitative Food Measurement*, 7(2), 41–56. DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-food-safety-chemistry-consortium.2023.1.

   This methods paper describes preparation of matrix-matched standards, blank correction and repeatability checks. Its scope is analytical measurement in prepared-food matrices. Vauzernac supervised the study; Rouvessac led the chemical measurements; Brzełowska reviewed the interpretation of the microbial reference work. The analytical procedures were subsequently used in the completed paired-lot study.

2. **Brzełowska, A.; Karszewicz, T.; Rouvessac, H.; Vauzernac, M.** (2024). 'Interpreting nonpathogenic surrogate growth during controlled refrigeration interruptions.' *Veterinary Food Process Studies*, 11(1), 15–29. DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-food-safety-chemistry-consortium.2024.1.

   The paper documents culture handling and the interpretation of surrogate growth in contained experiments conducted during 2023. It separates an experimental enumeration threshold from a regulatory criterion and explains why growth of the selected surrogate cannot establish the response of every foodborne pathogen.

3. **Velderschoot, S.; Drevenholt, L.; Vauzernac, M.** (2025). 'Replay and timestamp faults in laboratory cold-chain telemetry.' *Sensor Systems Security Methods*, 4(3), 88–103. DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-food-safety-chemistry-consortium.2025.1.

   This article presents the threat model and the 48-trace replay exercise reported in the final project report. Its contribution concerns gateway evidence and integrity rules. The evaluation uses archived laboratory traces, with attack construction and test conditions documented alongside the screening counts.

4. **Vauzernac, M.; Brzełowska, A.; Karszewicz, T.; Rouvessac, H.; Velderschoot, S.; Drevenholt, L.** (2026). 'Batch-held-out classification of surrogate growth from paired food measurements.' *Food Chain Measurement and Decisions*, 3(2), 61–79. DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-food-safety-chemistry-consortium.2026.1.

   Published on 14 August 2026, this article reports the 144 complete pairs from Mésurafroid-25. The analysis uses the project's paired-lot archive and grouped validation procedure. The article describes the sensitivity interval and limitations arising from missing measurements and controlled exposure conditions.

The final project report and the restricted dataset are held in the project archive. Their custody and access conditions are recorded in the final report and the signed data-use schedule.

# Staff, facilities, support and permissions

**Verified position at 30 September 2026.** This record describes existing resources and their current commitments.

## Staff and current allocation

The collaboration's relevant staff comprise 12 people with 8.4 full-time equivalents currently assigned to the laboratory, veterinary and security activities described here. These allocations are paid through existing contracts and national support.

| Organisation | Current staff allocation | Total FTE |
| --- | --- | --- |
| IIMAV | Coordinator 0.6; analytical chemist 1.0; microbiologist 1.0; statistician 0.8; process technician 0.6; data steward 0.2 | 4.2 |
| Rzewska Veterinary University | Veterinary lead 0.6; microbiologist 1.0; laboratory technician 0.8; quality officer 0.4 | 2.8 |
| Kelderspoor Sensorbeveiliging BV | Sensor systems engineer 0.8; security engineer 0.6 | 1.4 |

Mireille Vauzernac occupies the coordinator allocation; Hélène Rouvessac the analytical chemist allocation. Alicja Brzełowska is the veterinary lead and Tomasz Karszewicz the Polish microbiologist. Sander Velderschoot and Lotte Drevenholt hold the two Dutch allocations. There are no approved additional hires or outstanding instrument orders in this record.

## Existing facilities

Nantes houses a reference headspace gas chromatograph, a standards-preparation room, refrigerated storage and the calibration archive. Lyon houses the contained conveyor test line and programmable refrigeration chambers in room LY-P1. Its adjoining microbiology and analytical workspace, LY-M2, contains the study's headspace gas chromatograph, sampling station, culture facilities and waste-treatment equipment. Both Lyon rooms operate at containment level 1. Samples move between these adjoining rooms in closed secondary carriers. IIMAV's biological permissions are confined to these two rooms; Nantes handles non-inoculated analytical materials.

The Ghent establishment contains a liaison office and dry pilot room with gateway demonstrators and a telemetry display station. Its activities use electronic records and inert demonstration loads. Visiting staff remain within the IIMAV allocation above; the site has no separately assigned research team. Equipment expenditure and staff time enter IIMAV's accounts.

The Polish laboratory provides reference microbiology and independent review of plate records. As of 30 September 2026, the Rzewska laboratory operates at containment level 1 for nonpathogenic reference organisms and holds no pathogen-handling authorisation, including for Listeria monocytogenes. It has no food challenge-test protocol or process line, and no application to extend its biological permissions has been submitted. During Mésurafroid-25, study inoculation and enumeration were performed at Lyon; the Polish team's remote review used plate images, dilution records and instrument exports.

The Dutch SME maintains a telemetry replay bench and an isolated gateway test network. Its tools support packet inspection, timestamp manipulation, sequence checking and verification of signed messages. Message adapters permit use with different industrial sensor streams. The retained test library includes cold-chain traces with documented temperature profiles and synthetic messages for protocol testing. The partners use an access-controlled computing environment for statistical models and archived sensor records.

The current decision interface displays an advisory refrigeration alert, the measurements behind it and a record of the technician's response. A technician can reject or defer the alert and enter a reason. The interface is read-only with respect to equipment controls; equipment settings are entered separately by authorised staff.

## Biosafety and sample handling

The original protocol, **BS-IIMAV-22-11**, was approved on 14 November 2022 and covered the surrogate procedure from the start of Mésurafroid-25. It was replaced by **BS-IIMAV-24-06**, approved on 18 June 2024, following an update to recordkeeping and waste documentation. The replacement retained the organism, site and experimental scope. It was reviewed without scope extension on 10 September 2026 and remains active.

The authorised organism is the documented nonpathogenic strain **Lactococcus lactis IIMAV LL-07**. The protocol covers preparation, inoculation, opening, headspace sampling and enumeration in Lyon room LY-M2 at containment level 1, and movement of sealed sample vessels through the contained line in adjoining room LY-P1 at the same containment level. The organism schedule contains this strain only. All inoculated material remains within the Lyon research and waste route. No amendment submitted as of 30 September 2026.

The strain identity, inoculum preparation and disposal entries are recorded against each experimental batch. Technicians check vessel closure before line entry and reconcile vessels against the batch register at removal. Deviations are entered in the incident register and reviewed before the associated measurements are accepted into the analysis archive. The authorised procedure remains operational with existing staff and equipment.

There is no human dietary intervention in the collaboration's current work, and none is required for the contained measurement and process experiments. Current data describe food lots, instruments and laboratory operations. Technician response records use staff codes; the identification key is held locally with restricted access. These records are pseudonymised personal data.

## Current national support

IIMAV holds French ANR award ANR-PB-CAL26-004 of EUR 360,000 for calibration and laboratory quality work from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2028. Rzewska Veterinary University holds Polish National Science Centre award NCN-PB-RV24-011 of PLN 1,080,000 for reference microbiology from 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2027. The Dutch SME holds Netherlands Enterprise Agency national innovation support, reference RVO-PB-KS25-008, of EUR 180,000 for telemetry integrity work from 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2027. Each award is signed and active.

Staff time and equipment use are recorded against the relevant cost centre. The completed Mésurafroid-25 award is financially closed. Current allocations are committed to the activities specified in their respective award records.

The reported result pools these held-out predictions; it is not an evaluation of a single final model on a separate external population.

Of the 144 complete lots, 100 exceeded the reference endpoint and 44 did not. The classifier identified 81 of the 100 endpoint-positive lots and correctly classified 36 of the 44 endpoint-negative lots. Sensitivity was 0.81, with bootstrap 95% CI 0.72 to 0.88. Specificity was 0.82, rounded from 36/44. There were 19 false negatives and eight false positives.

The sensitivity interval used 10,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples of storage batches, preserving all lot records within each sampled batch. It describes uncertainty in the pooled held-out results under the study's batch structure. It does not include uncertainty from transfer to another food product, organism or commercial setting. The relatively high endpoint-positive proportion was created by the experimental exposure design and cannot be interpreted as commercial prevalence.

Two prespecified baselines used the same complete lots. A fixed time–temperature alarm identified 68 of the 100 positives and correctly classified 33 of the 44 negatives. A temperature-only logistic model identified 72 positives and correctly classified 34 negatives. These paired counts provide comparisons at the selected operating thresholds; the study did not establish a general superiority claim across all possible thresholds.

## Fault and security observations

An additional replay exercise used 48 recorded telemetry traces selected from the complete-lot archive. Twenty-four were retained unchanged and 24 were modified to repeat an earlier segment while retaining plausible temperatures. The initial integrity rule flagged 20 of the 24 modified traces and incorrectly flagged two of the 24 unchanged traces. These are laboratory screening counts from a deliberately balanced exercise, not field attack-detection rates.

The exercise exposed dependence on gateway timing and sequence information. It did not test an attacker controlling both the gateway credentials and its clock. There was no independent penetration test, no adaptive adversarial search and no assessment of robot control. The security findings were recorded separately from the food classifier's sensitivity.

## Interpretation and retained outputs

The work established a reproducible paired-measurement workflow and evidence of predictive association with surrogate growth under contained conditions. It did not measure avoided food loss, changes in commercial rejection rates, illness reduction or pathogen-specific hazard reduction. No food was sold or consumed, and no human dietary trial was conducted.

The archived dataset is titled 'Mésurafroid paired-lot release 1'. It contains lot identifiers, batch assignments, missingness reasons, reference counts, calibration records and telemetry. A research extract is shared among the partners under their data-use schedule. Supplier identifiers remain in IIMAV's restricted source register. The dataset has no public DOI and is not an unrestricted public release.

The principal limitations are the controlled food matrices, use of a single surrogate, incomplete observations, internal grouped validation and absence of commercial deployment. Technician decisions remained authoritative throughout: the interface supplied an alert and its supporting measurements, while the technician recorded acceptance, rejection or deferral.

# Staff, facilities, support and permissions

**Verified position at 30 September 2026.** This record describes existing resources and their current commitments. It is not an estimate of uncommitted capacity.

## Staff and current allocation

The collaboration's relevant staff comprise 12 people with 8.4 full-time equivalents currently assigned to the laboratory, veterinary and security activities described here. These allocations are paid through existing contracts and national support. They are not vacant posts or offers of additional staff time.

## Existing facilities

Nantes houses a headspace gas chromatograph, a microbiology preparation room, refrigerated storage and the calibration archive. Lyon houses the contained conveyor test line and programmable refrigeration chambers. The line accepts sealed sample vessels; its controls are isolated from commercial production. Equipment operation, cleaning and sample disposal are documented under IIMAV's internal quality system.

The Polish laboratory provides culture-based reference work and independent review of plate records. It has handled the study surrogate under the signed material-transfer terms. Possession of veterinary microbiology expertise does not confer authority to inoculate food in another organisation's premises.

The Dutch SME maintains a telemetry replay bench and an isolated gateway test network. Its existing tools support packet inspection, timestamp manipulation, sequence checking and verification of signed messages. The partners use an access-controlled computing environment for statistical models and archived sensor records. They have no dedicated robot-motion laboratory and no established programme for general industrial robot control.

The current decision interface displays an advisory refrigeration alert, the measurements behind it and a record of the technician's response. A technician can reject or defer the alert and enter a reason. The interface has no connection capable of commanding the contained line, a commercial vehicle or a packing machine. Existing capability therefore includes advisory cold-chain decisions and recorded human override.

## Biosafety and sample handling

IIMAV protocol **BS-IIMAV-24-06**, approved on 18 June 2024 and reviewed without scope extension on 10 September 2026, is active. It permits sealed samples containing the documented nonpathogenic surrogate on the contained test line only. Preparation, inoculation, opening and enumeration take place in the designated laboratory workspace. Line transport does not include open inoculated food. Samples are retained within the research waste route and are never released for consumption.

Live-pathogen inoculation on a commercial packing line is not authorised. As of 30 September 2026 there is no submitted amendment, pending application, external-site agreement or other permission covering that procedure. The active protocol cannot be treated as approval for a change of organism, containment or site. The authorised surrogate procedure remains operational with existing staff and equipment.

There is no human dietary intervention in the collaboration's current work, and none is required for the contained measurement and process experiments. Current data describe food lots, instruments and laboratory operations. Technician response records use staff codes; the identification key is held locally with restricted access. These records are not represented as fully anonymous personal data.

Each award is signed and active, rather than an application awaiting decision.

These awards support distinct recorded activities and are not combined into a single euro-denominated grant total. Staff time and equipment use are recorded against the relevant cost centre. The completed Mésurafroid-25 award is financially closed. None of the completed or current awards is Horizon Europe funding, and no current national allocation is recorded as an unspent contribution available for an unrelated action.

review_issues.problem: The visible files restate all three dossier-dependent trap premises as denials. T04: 'The Lyon branch cannot sign as an independent consortium member and does not represent a fourth entity or an additional country', 'References in laboratory records to a "Lyon partner" denote an internal operating unit', 'I do not hold a separate appointment at a legally independent Lyon institute'. review_issues.fix: Delete every sentence that names robots, robot actuation, a 'Lyon partner' or live-pathogen inoculation on a commercial line. State the scope positively and only once. For the legal table, the Lyon row should read 'operating site of IIMAV (no separate legal personality)'. review_issues.problem: The dossier makes the T14 premise implausible for this applicant. The PI is a food chemist whose CV and publications stress surrogate limits. The consortium has no access to any commercial packing line. No food microbiologist would propose inoculating a live pathogen on a commercial production line. The suggestion reads as constructed, not as a realistic overreach.
review_issues.fix: Move the premise to something this team might plausibly propose: a live-pathogen challenge test (for example Listeria monocytogenes, or Bacillus cereus for the rice matrix) on the contained Lyon line under BS-IIMAV-24-06. review_issues.where: consortium.md and resources.md (SME capabilities); planned task pub2-he-digital-stretch, T11
review_issues.problem: Nothing in the dossier would tempt a chemistry–veterinary–security consortium towards 'generic factory-robot motion control'. The pivot is not a realistic suggestion from this applicant, and it is only decidable because the dossier denies robot competence four times.
review_issues.fix: Anchor the scope drift in an existing asset. For example, the brief proposes making the SME's gateway replay and signed-telemetry tooling the deliverable as a generic industrial IoT/OT security product, with food-chain outcomes dropped. review_issues.problem: The missing-data pattern is engineered. All 16 incomplete lots fall one per seven-lot batch, none fall in the six-lot batches, every batch ends with exactly six complete lots, and the matrices split exactly 72/72. By chance this has probability of about 1e-8. It also contradicts the report's own statement that connector failures clustered during excursion handling, which would concentrate losses in excursion batches.
review_issues.fix: Report an irregular distribution. For example: the 16 incomplete lots fall in 11 batches (0–3 per batch, with more in 10 °C excursion batches); complete lots per batch range from 4 to 7; matrices split 70 rice and 74 poultry; outer folds hold 21–27 complete lots. Keep 144, 100/44 and all classification counts unchanged. Delete 'leaving six complete lots per batch'.

# Mireille Vauzernac — curriculum vitae

**Position:** Head of Food Measurement and Process Evidence, Institut indépendant des mesures alimentaires de Valmorin (IIMAV), Nantes, France.

**Record updated:** 30 September 2026.

## Education and appointments

I received my doctorate in analytical chemistry from the Université des Sciences de Montreval in 2005. My dissertation examined matrix effects in headspace measurements of chilled prepared foods, using paired chemical measurements and culture-based spoilage indicators. My earlier training was in chemistry, with laboratory placements in chromatographic method development.

From 2005 to 2013 I worked as a research chemist at IIMAV's Nantes branch. My responsibilities included calibration studies, reference-material preparation and investigating disagreement between rapid measurements and microbiological results. From 2013 to 2019 I led the institute's chilled-food measurement group. Since 2019 I have headed Food Measurement and Process Evidence, with responsibility for laboratory quality, statistical review and supervision of the institute's contained food-process test line.

## Research responsibilities

My work concerns the interpretation of measurements when food temperature histories are incomplete or unreliable. I have supervised studies combining volatile profiles, temperature records and microbial counts, and have signed the corresponding analytical validation reports. I distinguish a model's ability to reproduce a laboratory endpoint from evidence that its use changes a food-chain outcome.

I was principal investigator of Mésurafroid-25, conducted from January 2023 through December 2025. I approved its sampling protocol, chaired the review of missing observations and authorised release of its paired-lot research dataset. The completed study used laboratory food lots and a nonpathogenic surrogate. Its endpoint was surrogate growth under controlled refrigeration conditions.

I currently coordinate the technical relationship between IIMAV, Rzewska Veterinary University in Poland and Kelderspoor Sensorbeveiliging BV in the Netherlands. This role includes maintaining the agreement register, resolving measurement terminology and checking laboratory documentation. Each partner retains responsibility for its own staff and facilities.

## Methods, outputs and supervision

My practical expertise includes headspace gas chromatography, matrix-matched calibration, repeatability assessment and the interpretation of microbial reference measurements. I review statistical analysis plans covering grouped validation, missingness and bootstrap uncertainty. Model implementation and security assessment are undertaken with specialist colleagues.

My career publication record comprises 41 peer-reviewed articles. The separate collaboration register lists four articles published during 2023–2026. These include our calibration method, interpretation of surrogate growth, telemetry replay experiments and batch-held-out classification results.

I have supervised eight completed doctorates: five as principal supervisor and three as co-supervisor. Three further doctoral researchers remain registered under my co-supervision. I have supervised six completed postdoctoral appointments. These counts cover my career across projects and are separate from the current staff allocation recorded in the resources register.

My supervision has combined chemistry and veterinary microbiology, particularly the limits of surrogate organisms and the difference between an analytical alert and a food-release decision. I chaired IIMAV's analytical quality committee from 2016 to 2022 and have served on its research integrity committee since 2023. The quality committee maintained internal procedures for calibration traceability, duplicate measurements and reporting of detection limits.

**Principal investigator:** Mireille Vauzernac, IIMAV. Veterinary reference work was performed with Rzewska Veterinary University; telemetry assessment was performed with Kelderspoor Sensorbeveiliging BV.

## Funding and expenditure

The French Agence nationale de la recherche supported the project under award reference ANR-PB-MF25-017. The award and accepted eligible expenditure were both EUR 840,000. Expenditure comprised EUR 502,000 for personnel, EUR 118,000 for equipment and depreciation, EUR 104,000 for consumables, and EUR 116,000 for external analytical and data services. These categories sum to EUR 840,000. Partner service invoices are included in these categories and are not additional expenditure.

## Experimental question and material

The study examined whether chemical and temperature measurements could identify a predefined surrogate-growth endpoint after interrupted refrigeration. It did not estimate the prevalence of naturally occurring pathogens in retail food.

Technicians prepared 160 food lots: 80 cooked-rice lots and 80 cooked-poultry lots. A lot was a separately prepared food unit divided into matched analytical portions; repeated instrument readings and duplicate plates were not treated as independent lots. All material was designated for research and excluded from consumption.

The documented nonpathogenic strain Lactococcus lactis IIMAV LL-07 served as the sole biological surrogate. Preparation, inoculation, headspace sampling and microbial enumeration occurred in Lyon room LY-M2. Sealed sample vessels passed through the contained process line in adjoining room LY-P1. Refrigeration profiles included uninterrupted storage at 4 °C and controlled excursions to 10 °C. Samples were opened only in LY-M2.

Headspace measurements were made on the Lyon gas chromatograph. Nantes supplied calibration procedures and reviewed chromatograms electronically. Inoculated food remained at Lyon through analysis and disposal; the study therefore required no inter-site transfer of inoculated food. The protocol history is recorded in the resources register.

The 160 lots were processed in 24 storage batches. Sixteen batches contained seven lots and eight batches contained six lots. Batch membership recorded shared preparation and refrigeration conditions. Food matrix and temperature profile were recorded before outcome measurement.

## Measurements and analysis population

The reference endpoint was a final surrogate count above 6.0 log10 CFU/g. This was an experimental growth threshold, not a statutory food-safety limit. Enumeration used duplicate plates with documented dilution factors. Temperature histories and headspace chemical measurements supplied the model inputs. Matrix identity was included as a prespecified covariate.

There were 144 complete microbial and sensor pairs, representing 90% of the 160 lots. Ten lots lacked a usable sensor history and six lacked an interpretable reference count. These groups did not overlap. The 16 incomplete lots occurred in 11 batches: seven batches lost one lot, three lost two lots and one lost three lots. The remaining 13 batches had complete records. Complete lots per batch ranged from 4 to 7. The complete analysis population contained 70 rice lots and 74 poultry lots.

The missing records were retained in the archive with reason codes. Neither reference outcomes nor sensor histories were imputed for the classification analysis. Connector failures were more frequent during excursion handling, and incomplete records were concentrated in excursion batches. The excluded observations may have been more difficult to classify, so the complete-case results may be optimistic.

## Held-out classification results

Validation used six outer folds, each holding out four entire storage batches. The folds contained 21, 23, 24, 24, 25 and 27 complete lots, respectively. All preprocessing, feature selection and classifier fitting occurred using the other batches. Every complete lot received one prediction from a model that had not seen that lot or its storage batch. Threshold selection occurred within the training data. The reported result pools these held-out predictions; it is not an evaluation of a single final model on a separate external population.

Of the 144 complete lots, 100 exceeded the reference endpoint and 44 did not. The classifier identified 81 of the 100 endpoint-positive lots and correctly classified 36 of the 44 endpoint-negative lots. Sensitivity was 0.81, with bootstrap 95% CI 0.72 to 0.88. Specificity was 0.82, rounded from 36/44. There were 19 false negatives and eight false positives.

The sensitivity interval used 10,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples of storage batches, preserving all lot records within each sampled batch. It describes uncertainty in the pooled held-out results under the study's batch structure. It does not include uncertainty from transfer to another food product, organism or commercial setting. The relatively high endpoint-positive proportion was created by the experimental exposure design and cannot be interpreted as commercial prevalence.

Two prespecified baselines used the same complete lots. A fixed time–temperature alarm identified 68 of the 100 positives and correctly classified 33 of the 44 negatives. A temperature-only logistic model identified 72 positives and correctly classified 34 negatives. These paired counts provide comparisons at the selected operating thresholds; the study did not establish a general superiority claim across all possible thresholds.

## Fault and security observations

An additional replay exercise used 48 recorded telemetry traces selected from the complete-lot archive. Twenty-four were retained unchanged and 24 were modified to repeat an earlier segment while retaining plausible temperatures. The initial integrity rule flagged 20 of the 24 modified traces and incorrectly flagged two of the 24 unchanged traces. These are laboratory screening counts from a deliberately balanced exercise, not field attack-detection rates.

The exercise exposed dependence on gateway timing and sequence information. It did not test an attacker controlling both the gateway credentials and its clock. There was no independent penetration test or adaptive adversarial search. The security findings were recorded separately from the food classifier's sensitivity.

## Interpretation and retained outputs

The work established a reproducible paired-measurement workflow and evidence of predictive association with surrogate growth under contained conditions. It did not measure avoided food loss, changes in commercial rejection rates, illness reduction or pathogen-specific hazard reduction. No food was sold or consumed, and no human dietary trial was conducted.

The archived dataset is titled 'Mésurafroid paired-lot release 1'. It contains lot identifiers, batch assignments, missingness reasons, reference counts, calibration records and telemetry. A research extract is shared among the partners under their data-use schedule. Supplier identifiers remain in IIMAV's restricted source register. The dataset has no public DOI and is not an unrestricted public release.

The principal limitations are the controlled food matrices, use of a single surrogate, incomplete observations, internal grouped validation and absence of commercial deployment. Technician decisions remained authoritative throughout: the interface supplied an alert and its supporting measurements, while the technician recorded acceptance, rejection or deferral.

# Mireille Vauzernac — curriculum vitae

**Position:** Head of Food Measurement and Process Evidence, Institut indépendant des mesures alimentaires de Valmorin (IIMAV), Nantes, France.

**Record updated:** 30 September 2026.

## Education and appointments

I received my doctorate in analytical chemistry from the Université des Sciences de Montreval in 2005. My dissertation examined matrix effects in headspace measurements of chilled prepared foods, using paired chemical measurements and culture-based spoilage indicators. My earlier training was in chemistry, with laboratory placements in chromatographic method development.

From 2005 to 2013 I worked as a research chemist at IIMAV's Nantes branch. My responsibilities included calibration studies, reference-material preparation and investigating disagreement between rapid measurements and microbiological results. From 2013 to 2019 I led the institute's chilled-food measurement group. Since 2019 I have headed Food Measurement and Process Evidence, with responsibility for laboratory quality, statistical review and supervision of the institute's contained food-process test line.

## Research responsibilities

My work concerns the interpretation of measurements when food temperature histories are incomplete or unreliable. I have supervised studies combining volatile profiles, temperature records and microbial counts, and have signed the corresponding analytical validation reports. I distinguish a model's ability to reproduce a laboratory endpoint from evidence that its use changes a food-chain outcome.

I was principal investigator of Mésurafroid-25, conducted from January 2023 through December 2025. I approved its sampling protocol, chaired the review of missing observations and authorised release of its paired-lot research dataset. The completed study used laboratory food lots and a nonpathogenic surrogate. Its endpoint was surrogate growth under controlled refrigeration conditions.

I currently coordinate the technical relationship between IIMAV, Rzewska Veterinary University in Poland and Kelderspoor Sensorbeveiliging BV in the Netherlands. This role includes maintaining the agreement register, resolving measurement terminology and checking laboratory documentation. Each partner retains responsibility for its own staff and facilities.

## Methods, outputs and supervision

My practical expertise includes headspace gas chromatography, matrix-matched calibration, repeatability assessment and the interpretation of microbial reference measurements. I review statistical analysis plans covering grouped validation, missingness and bootstrap uncertainty. Model implementation and security assessment are undertaken with specialist colleagues.

My career publication record comprises 41 peer-reviewed articles. The separate collaboration register lists four articles published during 2023–2026. These include our calibration method, interpretation of surrogate growth, telemetry replay experiments and batch-held-out classification results.

I have supervised eight completed doctorates: five as principal supervisor and three as co-supervisor. Three further doctoral researchers remain registered under my co-supervision. I have supervised six completed postdoctoral appointments.

My supervision has combined chemistry and veterinary microbiology, particularly the limits of surrogate organisms and the difference between an analytical alert and a food-release decision. I chaired IIMAV's analytical quality committee from 2016 to 2022 and have served on its research integrity committee since 2023. The quality committee maintained internal procedures for calibration traceability, duplicate measurements and reporting of detection limits.

# Final scientific report: Mésurafroid-25

**Measurement agreement under interrupted refrigeration in prepared-food matrices**

**Project period:** 1 January 2023–31 December 2025. **Final report accepted:** 27 February 2026. **Archive status checked:** 30 September 2026.

**Principal investigator:** Mireille Vauzernac, IIMAV. Veterinary reference work was performed with Rzewska Veterinary University; telemetry assessment was performed with Kelderspoor Sensorbeveiliging BV.

## Funding and expenditure

The French Agence nationale de la recherche supported the project under award reference ANR-PB-MF25-017. The award and accepted eligible expenditure were both EUR 840,000. Expenditure comprised EUR 502,000 for personnel, EUR 118,000 for equipment and depreciation, EUR 104,000 for consumables, and EUR 116,000 for external analytical and data services.

## Experimental question and material

The study examined whether chemical and temperature measurements could identify a predefined surrogate-growth endpoint after interrupted refrigeration. It did not estimate the prevalence of naturally occurring pathogens in retail food.

Technicians prepared 160 food lots: 80 cooked-rice lots and 80 cooked-poultry lots. A lot was a separately prepared food unit divided into matched analytical portions; repeated instrument readings and duplicate plates were not treated as independent lots. All material was designated for research and excluded from consumption.

The documented nonpathogenic strain Lactococcus lactis IIMAV LL-07 served as the sole biological surrogate. Preparation, inoculation, headspace sampling and microbial enumeration occurred in Lyon room LY-M2. Sealed sample vessels passed through the contained process line in adjoining room LY-P1. Refrigeration profiles included uninterrupted storage at 4 °C and controlled excursions to 10 °C. Samples were opened only in LY-M2.

Headspace measurements were made on the Lyon gas chromatograph. Nantes supplied calibration procedures and reviewed chromatograms electronically. Inoculated food remained at Lyon through analysis and disposal; the study therefore required no inter-site transfer of inoculated food. The protocol history is recorded in the resources register.

The 160 lots were processed in 24 storage batches. Sixteen batches contained seven lots and eight batches contained six lots. Batch membership recorded shared preparation and refrigeration conditions. Food matrix and temperature profile were recorded before outcome measurement.

## Measurements and analysis population

The reference endpoint was a final surrogate count above 6.0 log10 CFU/g. This was an experimental growth threshold, not a statutory food-safety limit. Enumeration used duplicate plates with documented dilution factors. Temperature histories and headspace chemical measurements supplied the model inputs. Matrix identity was included as a prespecified covariate.

There were 144 complete microbial and sensor pairs, representing 90% of the 160 lots. Ten lots lacked a usable sensor history and six lacked an interpretable reference count. These groups did not overlap. The 16 incomplete lots occurred in 11 batches: seven batches lost one lot, three lost two lots and one lost three lots. The remaining 13 batches had complete records. Complete lots per batch ranged from 4 to 7. The complete analysis population contained 70 rice lots and 74 poultry lots.

The missing records were retained in the archive with reason codes. Neither reference outcomes nor sensor histories were imputed for the classification analysis. Connector failures were more frequent during excursion handling, and incomplete records were concentrated in excursion batches. The excluded observations may have been more difficult to classify, so the complete-case results may be optimistic.

## Held-out classification results

Validation used six outer folds, each holding out four entire storage batches. The folds contained 21, 23, 24, 24, 25 and 27 complete lots, respectively. All preprocessing, feature selection and classifier fitting occurred using the other batches. Every complete lot received one prediction from a model that had not seen that lot or its storage batch. Threshold selection occurred within the training data. The reported result pools these held-out predictions; it is not an evaluation of a single final model on a separate external population.

Of the 144 complete lots, 100 exceeded the reference endpoint and 44 did not. The classifier identified 81 of the 100 endpoint-positive lots and correctly classified 36 of the 44 endpoint-negative lots. Sensitivity was 0.81, with bootstrap 95% CI 0.72 to 0.88. Specificity was 0.82, rounded from 36/44. There were 19 false negatives and eight false positives.

The sensitivity interval used 10,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples of storage batches, preserving all lot records within each sampled batch. It describes uncertainty in the pooled held-out results under the study's batch structure. It does not include uncertainty from transfer to another food product, organism or commercial setting. The relatively high endpoint-positive proportion was created by the experimental exposure design and cannot be interpreted as commercial prevalence.

Two prespecified baselines used the same complete lots. A fixed time–temperature alarm identified 68 of the 100 positives and correctly classified 33 of the 44 negatives. A temperature-only logistic model identified 72 positives and correctly classified 34 negatives. These paired counts provide comparisons at the selected operating thresholds.

## Fault and security observations

An additional replay exercise used 48 recorded telemetry traces selected from the complete-lot archive. Twenty-four were retained unchanged and 24 were modified to repeat an earlier segment while retaining plausible temperatures. The initial integrity rule flagged 20 of the 24 modified traces and incorrectly flagged two of the 24 unchanged traces. These are laboratory screening counts from a deliberately balanced exercise, not field attack-detection rates.

The exercise exposed dependence on gateway timing and sequence information. It did not test an attacker controlling both the gateway credentials and its clock. There was no independent penetration test or adaptive adversarial search. The security findings were recorded separately from the food classifier's sensitivity.

## Interpretation and retained outputs

The work established a reproducible paired-measurement workflow and evidence of predictive association with surrogate growth under contained conditions. It did not measure avoided food loss, changes in commercial rejection rates, illness reduction or pathogen-specific hazard reduction. No food was sold or consumed, and no human dietary trial was conducted.

The archived dataset is titled 'Mésurafroid paired-lot release 1'. It contains lot identifiers, batch assignments, missingness reasons, reference counts, calibration records and telemetry. A research extract is shared among the partners under their data-use schedule. Supplier identifiers remain in IIMAV's restricted source register. The dataset has no public DOI and is not an unrestricted public release.

The principal limitations are the controlled food matrices, use of a single surrogate, incomplete observations, internal grouped validation and absence of commercial deployment. Technician decisions remained authoritative throughout: the interface supplied an alert and its supporting measurements, while the technician recorded acceptance, rejection or deferral.
